source: There are 17% excess birthday deaths compared to the average day difference.
claim: In 2000, 183 of the 57,010 deaths occurred on birthdays, 17.2% above the 156.2 average deaths per day difference.
code: d[d.death.str.startswith('2000')].days_from_birthday.value_counts().to_frame('deaths').assign(total=lambda x: x.deaths.sum(), average=lambda x: x.deaths.mean(), excess_pct=lambda x: (x.deaths/x.deaths.mean()-1)*100).loc[[0]]

source: Did you notice that just 12 days after birthday deaths is nearly as high?
claim: In 2000, 12 days after the birthday had 181 deaths, nearly as many as the 183 on the birthday itself.

source: You can see that birthdays (day difference = 0) have one of the highest death frequencies.
claim: In 2000, the birthday's 183 deaths ranked eighth among the 365 day differences.

source: In the chart above, there are eight day differences with values between 180-185, including birthday deaths.
claim: In 2000, eight day differences had between 180 and 185 deaths, including the birthday's 183.

source: If we measure the spread, we find that many values–about 68%–fall within a certain range (+/- 13) of the average (156 deaths). This range (143-169) is what statisticians call one standard deviation.
claim: In 2000, the 365 daily death counts average 156.2 with a standard deviation of 12.8, so one standard deviation spans 143.4 to 169.0.
code: d[d.death.str.startswith('2000')].days_from_birthday.value_counts().to_frame('deaths').assign(average=lambda x: x.deaths.mean(), sd=lambda x: x.deaths.std(), low=lambda x: x.deaths.mean()-x.deaths.std(), high=lambda x: x.deaths.mean()+x.deaths.std()).loc[[0]].T

source: We expect most (95%) values to fall within two standard deviations. That means anything from 130-182 is normal variation–expected random noise in our data. Birthday deaths are a hair higher, at just over 2 standard deviations.
claim: In 2000, 95.1% of daily death counts fall within two standard deviations, from 130.5 to 181.9, and the birthday's 183 deaths are 2.09 standard deviations above the 156.2 average.
code: d[d.death.str.startswith('2000')].days_from_birthday.value_counts().to_frame('deaths').assign(average=lambda x: x.deaths.mean(), sd=lambda x: x.deaths.std(), low2=lambda x: x.deaths.mean()-2*x.deaths.std(), high2=lambda x: x.deaths.mean()+2*x.deaths.std(), pct_2sd=lambda x: x.deaths.between(x.deaths.mean()-2*x.deaths.std(), x.deaths.mean()+2*x.deaths.std()).mean()*100, z0=lambda x: (x.loc[0,'deaths']-x.deaths.mean())/x.deaths.std()).loc[[0]].T

source: Some years, like 1999, will show a strong birthday effect.
claim: In 1999 there were 191 birthday deaths, 24.2% above the 153.7 average deaths per day difference.
code: d[d.death.str.startswith('1999')].days_from_birthday.value_counts().to_frame('deaths').assign(total=lambda x: x.deaths.sum(), average=lambda x: x.deaths.mean(), excess_pct=lambda x: (x.deaths/x.deaths.mean()-1)*100).loc[[0]]

source: While other years, like 2002, might show nothing at all.

claim: Across all 1,955,588 deaths, 5,728 occurred on birthdays, 6.9% above the 5,357.8 average deaths per day difference.

claim: With 5,728 birthday deaths against a 5,357.8 average and a 74.2 standard deviation, the z-score is 5.0.
code: d.days_from_birthday.value_counts().to_frame('deaths').assign(average=lambda x: x.deaths.mean(), sd=lambda x: x.deaths.std(), z=lambda x: (x.deaths-x.deaths.mean())/x.deaths.std()).loc[[0]]

source: Our p-value is ~0.000001, meaning there’s less than a 0.0001% chance we’d see this birthday effect if deaths were actually random.

Take January in Massachusetts: 8.5% of people are born then, but 9.6% of all deaths happen in January. This means January-born people would naturally show 13% more birthday deaths just because January is a high-mortality month–regardless of some birthday effect.
claim: January accounts for 165,570 births (8.5%) and 187,356 deaths (9.6%), so its death share is 1.13 times its birth share.
code: pd.DataFrame({'births': d.birth.str[5:7].value_counts(), 'deaths': d.death.str[5:7].value_counts()}).assign(birth_pct=lambda x: x.births/x.births.sum()*100, death_pct=lambda x: x.deaths/x.deaths.sum()*100, ratio=lambda x: x.death_pct/x.birth_pct).loc[['01']].T

source: After plugging in the numbers, we get an expected value of 5,355 birthday deaths, and observation of 5,728 deaths. There are 7.0% excess birthday deaths in Massachusetts.
claim: Accounting for each day's birth and death shares gives 5,354.9 expected birthday deaths against 5,728 observed, a 7.0% excess.
code: (d.assign(bday=pd.to_datetime(d.birth.str[5:], format='%m-%d', errors='coerce').dt.dayofyear, dday=pd.to_datetime(d.death.str[5:], format='%m-%d', errors='coerce').dt.dayofyear).pipe(lambda x: pd.crosstab(x.bday,x.dday)).pipe(lambda m: pd.DataFrame({'expected': m.sum(axis=1)*m.sum(axis=0)/m.values.sum(), 'observed': np.diag(m)}).sum().to_frame().T.assign(excess_pct=lambda y: (y.observed/y.expected-1)*100)))

source: The only additional noteworthy finding after stratification was that accidental deaths showed 35% excess deaths on birthdays in Massachusetts, supporting a theory around celebratory behavior.
claim: Among the 77,770 accidental deaths, 288 occurred on birthdays, 35.2% above the 213.1 average deaths per day difference.
